results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve); kFLC index accepted as an alternative to CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting MRI markers; additional supporting evidence recommended in people over 50 or with vascular risk factors.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Consensus MRI protocol for suspected MS: brain MRI with 3D FLAIR, T2, DWI and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and spinal cord MRI at diagnosis; gadolinium at baseline to show active lesions.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on a single cerebellar lesion or a single clinical event without confirming dissemination in space and time per the 2024 revised McDonald criteria
Do not interpret ANA 1:80 speckled with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies as SLE or CNS lupus: this titre occurs in healthy people and in MS, and he has no systemic features
Do not treat the open-ring enhancing peduncle lesion as a neoplasm or abscess for surgery or biopsy when its morphology, the other typical lesions and the CSF favour demyelination
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria: two attacks (left leg episode 14 months ago matching the C3-C4 cord lesion, current cerebellar attack) with DIS in four regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and enhancing and non-enhancing lesions

Treat the disabling cerebellar relapse with methylprednisolone oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days, after excluding infection, with blood pressure monitoring while he is hypertensive; plasma exchange if a disabling relapse does not respond
Refer for physiotherapy and assess falls risk for the cerebellar gait ataxia (cannot tandem walk)
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 14 months, an enhancing 18 mm peduncle lesion)

Before natalizumab, check anti-JCV antibody status and index; before an anti-CD20 or S1P modulator, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV antibody and VZV IgG (HIV already negative); give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting

avoided_actions.rationale: He has had no seizure or alteration of awareness; EEG does not inform a cerebellar lesion.
The posterior fossa lesion is assessed with MRI; CT is degraded by artefact there and does not characterise demyelination.
No restricted diffusion and an inflammatory lesion pattern leave no cardioembolic question to answer.
No palpitations, syncope or infarct on MRI; rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
FDG-PET does not distinguish an enhancing demyelinating lesion from a neoplasm reliably and adds nothing to MRI and CSF in this case.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward cerebellar-onset RRMS in a middle-aged Black African man. DIS (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial on brain MRI; spinal cord on spine MRI) and DIT (simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions) are both established, with OCB-positive CSF supportive. The main challenge is the low-titre ANA (1:80 speckled), which must not be over-read as CNS lupus without systemic features or specific antibodies.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Typical RRMS with cerebellar onset: DIS in 4 of 5 regions, DIT by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; a prior cord attack misattributed to disc disease; one clinically grounded red herring (low-titre ANA).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kwame Asante is a 43-year-old right-handed Ghanaian man who presents with a 2-week history of progressive right-sided limb incoordination and slurred speech. He first noticed difficulty writing on the classroom blackboard approximately 14 days ago, when his right hand began missing its target and producing jerky, inaccurate movements. Over the following days he developed an unsteady walking pattern, describing a feeling that his legs were not working together and that he was veering to the right. He also noticed that his speech had become slurred and he was occasionally stumbling over words, which his students and wife had remarked upon. He denies diplopia, facial numbness or weakness, dysphagia, limb weakness, sensory loss, urinary or bowel symptoms, or headache. He has no fever, weight loss, night sweats, rash, oral ulcers, or joint pain. He reports that approximately 14 months ago he experienced a 6-week episode of numbness and a heavy, weak feeling in his left leg, which gradually resolved without specific treatment. At that time, a general practitioner examined him and attributed the symptoms to lumbar disc disease; no imaging was performed. He has otherwise been well. He emigrated from Ghana to the United Kingdom 8 years ago. He has no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. He denies any prior episodes of visual loss, diplopia, or neurological symptoms apart from the leg episode 14 months ago. His hypertension has been stable on amlodipine. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substances. Review of systems is notable only for mild, intermittent fatigue over the past 6 months that he attributed to workload stress.
